bipartite.kami_theme: The passage of spring into summer, inferred as a temporal/seasonal statement ("haru sugite natsu ki ni kerashi" - spring has passed, it seems summer has come)
bipartite.shimo_theme: The visual detail of white robes being spread to dry on Mount Kagu, which serves as the sensory evidence confirming summer's arrival
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku states the seasonal transition as an inference (‑けらし, 'it seems/must be'), and the shimo-no-ku supplies the concrete sensory evidence (the customary sight/report of white summer robes drying on Kaguyama) that grounds and confirms that inference. The whole poem is structured as: conclusion (spring has given way to summer) supported by observed/reported proof (robes drying), rather than one half causing the other physically.

makurakotoba.conventional_meaning: white cloth/white mulberry-bark cloth; a fixed epithet establishing whiteness and textile purity, conventionally preceding words for white garments, snow, clouds

kigo.note: The explicit statement that summer has arrived is itself the seasonal marker; combined with 白妙の衣ほすてふ (the custom of airing/drying white robes in early summer, per court custom recorded near Mount Kagu), it fixes the poem firmly as a summer poem marking the seasonal changeover from spring, a common structural theme in the Kokinshū and later imperial anthologies where the first summer poem announces the season's arrival
